newsitem.title: UK: 1996/7 cocoa deficit could near 50,000 T - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: 1996/7 cocoa deficit could near 50,000 T - Merrill.

text.p: The 1996/97 cocoa deficit could drop to about 50,000 tonnes due to improving Ivorian crop prospects and indications of slower-than-expected demand, said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.
Ganes said the total Ivorian crop might not be much less than last season's bumper harvest of 1.2 million tonnes.

April rains have "vastly improved mid-crop expectations, with some suggesting that output might even be better than last season," she said. "This is supported by reports that the bean sizes are also bigger than last season."

On May 1, the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) cut its forecast for this year's cocoa deficit to 115,000 tonnes from last year's 160,000-tonnes surplus, which Ganes said was "a far cry from estimates at the start of the year calling for a deficit of more than 200,000 tonnes."

But she said Merrill Lynch believes "the deficit could shrink further and, in the end, be closer to 50,000 tonnes based on the improving Ivorian crop prospects. Moreover, with adequate rainfall, there seems to be little reason to expect the 1997/98 main crop to be reduced."
In addition to expectations of swollen supply, Ganes said "demand does not seem to be growing at the robust pace some had earlier anticipated."

With modest growth in usage expected next year, she said "stocks might fall, but the stocks/use ratio might not be at levels considered 'dangerously low,' which would spark fears of a shortfall and push prices up sharply."

As a result, Merrill Lynch feels the market is overpriced with New York cocoa futures above $1,450 per tonne. A fairer value for New York cocoa futures should be about $75 to $100 per tonne lower, Ganes said.
